title-group.article-title: A step towards modelling amyotrophic lateral sclerosis in primates

abstract.p: A new primate model offers a promising first step towards reproducing the spread of ALS pathology across synapses, although important differences from the stereotyped patterns observed in human disease remain to be addressed.

boxed-text.p: Related research article Jones RHA, Saieva L, Balezeau F, Schofield I, McCardle C, Baker MR, Baker SN. 2026. A non-human primate model of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. eLife 15:RP109810. doi: 10.7554/eLife.109810.

body.p: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rapidly progressing neurodegenerative disease characterised by the degeneration of motor neurons. Previous research has shown that ALS and also Alzheimer’s disease target structures unique to the human central nervous system, such as the monosynaptic corticospinal tract (CST) in the motor cortex and the transentorhinal cortex, respectively (Braak and Del Tredici, 2011).

This fuelled the hypothesis that these diseases may be specific to humans, highlighting the limitations of rodent models, which do not fully replicate human neuroanatomy or the deficits associated with these neurodegenerative conditions (Braak et al., 2013; Brettschneider et al., 2013). Furthermore, this hypothesis suggests that disease pathology propagates in a prion-like manner: misfolded proteins can induce neighbouring proteins to adopt the same abnormal structure, allowing spread between connected cells – similar to the spread of infectious pathogens, although actual infectivity has never been demonstrated.

Accumulations of misfolded proteins are a hallmark of neurodegenerative diseases. In ALS, this predominantly affects the protein TDP-43. These pathological changes appear to spread among close but also more distant neural regions, along the monosynaptic corticospinal tract from the motor cortex to the brainstem and spinal cord (Lemon and Griffiths, 2005; Witham et al., 2016). This trajectory is also consistent with the pattern of muscle weakness observed in ALS (Ludolph et al., 2020). However, the molecular mechanisms and the precise direction of this pathological spread have so far been unclear.

Now, in eLife, Stuart Baker and colleagues at Newcastle University – including Rachael Jones as first author – modelled these principles in two rhesus macaques (Jones et al., 2026). The researchers overexpressed the protein TDP-43 in motor neurons supplying a forearm muscle in two female rhesus macaques and used T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to monitor changes in muscle signal intensity, which can indicate muscle denervation and motor neuron degeneration.

The results revealed abnormal signal changes in the brachioradialis muscle, consistent with muscle denervation (loss of nerve supply) caused by motor neuron degeneration (Figure 1). Autopsy findings also showed pTDP-43 deposits in the cervical spinal cord and both sides of the motor cortex. In principle, this model could help bridge the gap between human disease and experimental animal research. However, it currently fails to reproduce three major features identified in previous studies as relevant to ALS pathology (Brettschneider et al., 2013; Braak et al., 2013; Fatima et al., 2015; Braak et al., 2017).

caption.title: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis in humans and macaques.
caption.p: In people, ALS pathology spreads from the motor cortex along the corticospinal tract to motor neurons in the brainstem and the spinal cord. In the macaque model, TDP-41 was overexpressed in the motor neurons of a forearm muscle (brachioradialis). Autopsies revealed pTDP-43 deposits in the cervical spinal cord and in both sides of the motor cortex of macaques. In human ALS, no neuroanatomical evidence for the spread from the spinal cord back to the motor cortex has been found.

body.p: First, these studies suggest that ALS primarily affects corticofugal tracts (which carry signals away from the cerebral cortex), with disease pathology spreading from the motor cortex to the spinal cord and bulbar motor neurons along the corticospinal tract. There is presently no neuroanatomical evidence supporting the reverse direction of spread, from the spinal cord backwards to the cortex.

Although Jones et al. reported the pathological spread of damaged pTDP-43, they did not show that it followed the direct, one-to-one connections between neurons, which is characteristic of the human corticospinal system and its physiology. However, it is currently not known whether a direct monosynaptic pathway exists between the cortex and the motor neuron pool of the brachioradialis in macaques. Future experiments could address this question by examining muscles with well-established monosynaptic connections, such as the biceps brachii, wrist and finger extensors or the small hand muscles.

Another important but commonly overlooked feature of human ALS is that pTDP-43 pathology is generally not detected within the corticospinal tract itself. This contrasts with reports of pTDP-43 pathology in the motor axons of spinal anterior horn cells and the bulbar motor neurons. Studies have instead found pTDP-43 aggregates in oligodendrocytes surrounding the corticospinal fibres (Braak et al., 2017).

It is tempting to speculate that phosphorylation of TDP-43 is a form of detoxification by affecting its ability to spread between cells and potentially limiting its passage across synapses. Non-phosphorylated TDP-43 might be transferred between connected neurons and become phosphorylated only after entering the recipient cells. Alternatively, pTDP-43 may simply not be able to cross synapses. This could explain why pTDP-43 pathology is found in connected neuronal populations without necessarily being detectable within the intervening corticospinal axons. However, more research would be needed to investigate this possibility.

These three principles should ultimately be demonstrated in a primate model that reproduces the stereotyped pattern of disease spread observed in human ALS. Clearly, much experimental work remains before this goal can be achieved. However, Jones et al. are to be applauded for taking a first step toward a primate model of ALS. They have clearly understood the key messages from previous neuroanatomical studies and demonstrated that their approach can model the spread of pathological changes across synapses.
